generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this shows up the same way in any subject: rereading your notes or a chapter leaves the material feeling familiar, yet an exam asks you to produce it, not just recognise it. Rebuilding an idea from memory, explaining it in your own words, and testing yourself on it force a deeper kind of processing that rereading never reaches. The small habit of working with knowledge, rather than looking it over, is what separates revision that holds from revision that fades.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who set aside the same hours to revise the same demanding topic.

{{learner-a}} spends the time reading. They read the chapter twice and highlight the key points, and it feels like steady progress because every page has been covered. But they produce nothing: no diagram, no self-test, no explanation in their own words. When a past question asks them to set the topic out, the material feels familiar yet strangely hard to reproduce. This is passive revision.

{{learner-b}} reads the same chapter once, then closes it. They rebuild the topic from memory as a diagram, turn each gap into a test question, and explain the whole thing aloud without looking. Every gap that surfaces sends them back to the chapter with a clear purpose. By the end they can reproduce and explain the topic, not just recognise it. This is active revision.

Both students spent the same hours. Only {{learner-b}} turned those hours into knowledge that would survive the exam, by producing and testing the material rather than only reading it.
generatedProse.summary: Active revision is a different kind of work with your material, not simply more time spent on it. You can now contrast active and passive revision and explain why producing and testing an idea deepens it, and you can judge whether an approach is genuinely active. Whatever you are studying, the test is the same: are you reproducing and checking the material, or only looking it over? The next lesson turns this principle into the specific techniques you can choose from.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s revision active rather than passive?

items.text: {{learner-b}} rebuilt the topic from memory and tested it, returning to the chapter only to fix the gaps.
{{learner-b}} read the chapter more carefully than {{learner-a}}.
{{learner-b}} highlighted the key points in the chapter.

feedback.correct: That's right. Producing and testing the material, then returning to the chapter to fix gaps, is what made it active.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} did with the material, beyond reading it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} rebuilt the topic from memory and tested it, returning to the chapter only to fix gaps. Extra hours, more careful reading and highlighting all stay passive.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
